activities.caption: pair each melting trick with where it operates
activities.name: volcMeltMatch

config.prompt: Pair each melting trick with where it operates and what it makes:

pairs.right: plates diverge or a plume rises — most of the world's basalt
subducting plates release water — the sticky arc magmas of the Ring of Fire
hot magma melts cooler crust — the route to rhyolite and granite

config.why: One physical system, three triggers — and the whole diversity of volcanic behaviour follows from which trigger fired.

config.prompt: File each property under the magma family it describes:

items.label: cools fast into the rock of every ocean floor
usually never erupts, cooling slowly into granite

config.why: Composition and cooling rate are written in the texture: slow cooling means large crystals, fast cooling means microscopic ones.

activities.caption: call the size of the last super-eruption
activities.name: volcYellowEst

config.prompt: Yellowstone's last caldera-forming eruption, 640,000 years ago, ejected about how much rock?
config.why: About 1,000 km³ — twice the volume of Lake Erie, in one event.
config.context: a stratovolcano's big eruption moves single cubic kilometres

activities.caption: true or false — where the planet's lava actually flows
activities.name: volcRidgeJudge

config.statement: Most of Earth's volcanic output happens at the deadly Ring of Fire arcs, where people can watch it.
config.why: False — the majority of Earth's volcanic output is at the mid-ocean ridge system, entirely underwater and almost unwatched, building new oceanic crust along 65,000 km of ridge.

activities.anchor: Lava is the hazard everybody pictures
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — what actually kills
activities.name: volcHazardSpot

config.prompt: One of these hazard claims is backwards — click it:
lines: Pyroclastic flows run at 100–700 km/h and 300–700 °C, incinerating everything in their path.
Lahars need no eruption — loose ash plus rain or a melted glacier, at highway speed down river valleys.
Lava flows are the deadliest hazard, killing thousands in most eruptions.
Ashfall collapses roofs, ruins engines and crops, and grounds aviation.
config.correction: Lava is the hazard almost nobody dies of — it moves slowly enough to outrun; the killers are pyroclastic flows, lahars, ashfall and gas.
config.why: The hazard that kills is rarely the one in the picture — which is why hazard maps, not heroics, are modern volcanology's main product.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the four signals a restless volcano sends
activities.name: volcSignalsCloze

config.text: A restless volcano announces itself four ways: %%0%% — swarms of small earthquakes rising toward the surface; %%1%% — the volcano inflates as magma fills it, resolved to millimetres by InSAR satellites; %%2%% chemistry — SO₂ output rising as fresh magma nears; and %%3%% or remote sensing of the warming ground.
config.hint: Cracking rock, a swelling flank, a changing sniff, and a warmer-than-usual surface.

activities.anchor: alarm too often and the public stops listening
activities.caption: walk the forecaster's line
activities.name: volcForecastBranch

config.root: Restless volcano: seismic swarms rising, gas climbing, millimetres of bulge — but most intrusions stall at depth and cool.

start.text: Three hundred thousand people live in the valleys. What do you recommend?

choices.label: Order the evacuation now
choices.feedback: Pinatubo's standard: the 1991 evacuation saved an estimated 5,000–20,000 lives — but alarm too often and the public stops listening.

choices.label: Wait for certainty before alarming anyone
choices.feedback: Armero's failure mode: warnings issued and unheeded, about 23,000 dead when the lahar arrived.

choices.label: Evacuate only the nearest villages
choices.feedback: Partial evacuation buys time — but the pyroclastic flow's geography, not the map's rings, decides who is in range.

pinatubo.text: The evacuation holds for weeks; the eruption comes Plinian-scale. Trust survives because the forecast was right — this time.

choices.label: What if the intrusion had stalled?
choices.feedback: Then the next alarm is trusted a little less — the boy-who-cried-wolf budget is real.

armero.text: Certainty arrived with the mudflow. Forecasting too late is the same as not forecasting.

partial.text: The hazard map, not the radius, sets the zone — lahars run river valleys kilometres from the vent.

wolf.text: Every false alarm spends trust; every delayed one spends lives. That is the line forecasters walk.

config.why: Forecasting is a social technology built on geophysical instruments — the geophysics is the easy half.

activities.anchor: No lava ever entered the city
activities.caption: the picture versus the reality — drag the divider
activities.name: volcPompeiiCompare

config.prompt: What killed Pompeii — the picture and the reality:

before.label: the picture
before.text: a river of lava swallowing the city — the image almost everyone carries

after.label: the reality
after.text: ashfall collapsing roofs, then pyroclastic surges sweeping the region on the eruption's second day

config.why: The confusion is instructive precisely because it hides the real lesson: the hazard that kills is rarely the one in the picture.

config.prompt: Rebuild the Pinatubo sequence — what came first:
items: April–June 1991: seismic swarms, inflation, rising SO₂ and thermal anomalies all appear
Forecasts predict a major eruption within days
Tens of thousands of people and the local US air base are evacuated
15 June: a Plinian eruption — the second-largest of the 20th century
config.why: The evacuation is estimated to have saved 5,000–20,000 lives — volcanology cannot stop an eruption, but it can move the people out of the way.
